definition: To protest or criticize something strongly and angrily, in speech or writing.
example: Every week the old columnist would inveigh against the roar of leaf blowers at dawn.
nuance: To inveigh is to rail against something, usually followed by "against"; inveigle means to coax someone with flattery or trickery.
prompt: A town council proposes paving over the only public park to build a parking lot.
options: Residents packed the meeting to inveigh against paving the park.
A developer tried to inveigh the council into approving the lot by praising their wisdom.
The mayor rose to inveigh in favor of the lot, praising every detail of the design.
By noon the work crew had begun to inveigh the park, pouring concrete over the lawn.
reasons: Crowding in to protest the plan loudly is exactly this kind of angry public objection.
Winning someone over with flattery is inveigle, a look-alike word, not inveigh.
The word expresses hostility, so it cannot describe enthusiastic support.
The word describes harsh words of protest, not a physical act like laying pavement.

practice.prompt: A food critic is fed up with restaurants serving tiny, overpriced portions.
options: Delighted, the critic would inveigh against the meal as the finest she had ever eaten.
The waiter set out a kitchen scale to inveigh each portion before it left the kitchen.
In her column, the critic chose to inveigh against plates holding three peas and a dot of sauce.
The chef hoped to inveigh the critic into a kind review by sending out free desserts.
reasons: Calling a meal the finest ever is high praise, the reverse of angry condemnation.
Despite the spelling, the word has nothing to do with weighing anything.
Using her column to attack a trend she dislikes is a fitting case of fierce criticism.
Luring someone with gifts or charm is inveigle; the two words are often mixed up.
